questions.question: The new flag of revolutionary France was the ____.
Napoleon's Civil Code was passed in the year ____.
Germany was unified under Otto von ____.
Italy's volunteer leader who marched into South Italy in 1860 was ____.
The female allegory of France was called ____.
What measures did the French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity among the French?
questions.answer: They emphasised the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and the citoyen (the citizen). They introduced a new tricolour flag, replaced the Estates General with an elected National Assembly, set up a centralised administration with uniform laws, abolished internal customs duties, adopted a uniform system of weights and measures, and made French (as spoken in Paris) the common national language.

questions.question: Explain the main features of Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804.
questions.answer: (i) It abolished all privileges based on birth. (ii) It established equality before the law. (iii) It secured the right to private property. (iv) Where Napoleon ruled, it abolished feudalism, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, and removed guild restrictions. (v) It introduced uniform administrative divisions and laws — facilitating trade and the movement of goods and capital.
questions.explanation: Five features of the Code Napoleon.

questions.question: What role did the educated middle class and the Romantic movement play in spreading nationalism in 19th-century Europe?
questions.answer: The new EDUCATED MIDDLE CLASS — entrepreneurs, professionals, students, journalists — championed liberty, equality before the law, and constitutional government, and led nationalist movements. ROMANTICISM emphasised emotion, intuition and folk culture. Romantic artists, poets and thinkers (like Herder) argued that the true spirit of a nation lived in its language, folk songs and folk poetry. Together, the middle-class political programme and the Romantic cultural programme gave NATIONALISM both its political demands and its emotional power.

questions.question: Briefly describe how Italy was unified.
questions.answer: Italy was politically fragmented into seven states. Mazzini's 'Young Italy' movement failed. Then the Sardinian king Victor Emmanuel II and his minister Count Cavour, through diplomacy and an alliance with France, defeated Austria in 1859. Garibaldi led armed volunteers into South Italy in 1860 and won over the local peasants, driving out the Spanish Bourbons. In 1861, Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of UNITED ITALY.
questions.explanation: Mazzini → Cavour + diplomacy → Garibaldi + the south → 1861.

questions.question: How did artists portray nations as female allegories? Give two examples.
questions.answer: In the 19th century, artists personified nations as female figures called allegories. (i) MARIANNE represented FRANCE — wearing the red cap of liberty, holding the tricolour and the cockade. Her statues were placed in public squares; her image appeared on coins and stamps. (ii) GERMANIA represented GERMANY — wearing a crown of oak leaves, the German oak symbolising heroism. The female allegory linked the nation with values of liberty and motherhood and gave it a face citizens could love.

questions.question: Why did the Balkans become a region of intense conflict in the late 19th and early 20th centuries?
questions.answer: The Balkans was a region of geographical and ethnic variation, populated mainly by Slavs. A large part of it was under the OTTOMAN EMPIRE. As the Ottoman Empire DECLINED from the 1870s, the various Slavic nationalities — Serbs, Bulgars, Croats, etc. — claimed independent nation-states based on history and identity, often making CONFLICTING claims to the same territory. Each Balkan state was jealous of the others. At the same time, the great European powers — Russia, Germany, England, Austria-Hungary — were rivals over trade, colonies and military might, and they each tried to USE Balkan nationalisms for their own imperial purposes. These rivalries finally exploded in the FIRST WORLD WAR (1914).
questions.explanation: Ethnic mosaic + Ottoman decline + great-power rivalry.

questions.question: Discuss the major liberal-nationalist uprisings of 1830 and 1848 in Europe. To what extent were they successful?
questions.answer: 1830s — economic hardship, population growth, urban migration, machine-made goods displacing craftsmen, and feudal dues on peasants combined with the demand for liberal-nationalist constitutions. The JULY REVOLUTION in France (1830) overthrew the Bourbons and installed Louis Philippe. Belgium broke away from the Netherlands the same year. Greece won independence from the Ottoman Empire (Treaty of Constantinople, 1832), aided by Romantic European sympathy (e.g. Lord Byron). 1848 — fresh food shortages and unemployment triggered uprisings in Paris, Vienna, Berlin and Italian states. Workers and peasants demanded relief; the educated middle classes pressed for nationalist constitutions. In Frankfurt, an all-German parliament drafted a constitution, but it was rejected by Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia and the assembly was forced to disband. ASSESSMENT — most 1848 revolutions were politically DEFEATED. But they had two lasting effects: (i) they made the demand for constitutional, liberal nation-states impossible to ignore — even monarchies began to grant constitutions; (ii) they showed that nationalism could no longer be repressed indefinitely. The actual unification of Italy and Germany came two decades later — by conservative state-building rather than by liberal revolution.

questions.question: Trace how nationalism in Europe shifted from a liberal-democratic ideal in the early 19th century to a narrow, imperialist creed by the end of the century. Use specific examples.
questions.answer: EARLY 19TH CENTURY — nationalism was linked with LIBERTY and DEMOCRACY. It demanded constitutional government, equality before the law, civil rights and the abolition of feudal privileges. The 1830 and 1848 revolutions, the Greek war of independence and the Italian Risorgimento all expressed this liberal-democratic ideal. Romantic thinkers like Herder linked nation to folk culture and language; Mazzini's Young Italy was openly republican. SECOND HALF — nationalism was harnessed by CONSERVATIVES for STATE-BUILDING. Bismarck's wars (1864, 1866, 1870–71) and Cavour's diplomacy unified Germany and Italy without democratic revolution. The new states emphasised modern administration, modern armies and economic uniformity — but were NOT especially democratic. LATE 19TH CENTURY — nationalism became a narrow creed: nationalist groups grew INTOLERANT of each other, ever ready to go to war. European powers manipulated the nationalist aspirations of subject peoples in the Balkans to FURTHER their own IMPERIALIST aims (Russia among the Slavs, Austria-Hungary in the western Balkans, Germany backing Austria, England guarding its routes). The Balkan states were jealous of one another; great-power rivalries over trade, colonies and arms grew sharper. These rivalries detonated in the FIRST WORLD WAR (1914). Thus the same word — NATIONALISM — moved from being a CALL FOR FREEDOM in 1789–1848 to being a CALL FOR EMPIRE AND WAR by 1900.
